q: You are planning your first trade-wind crossing from the Canaries to the Caribbean. When do you leave?
a: Late November to January
o: June, with the longest days
August, the calmest month
September, the warmest sea
why: Leave as the hurricane season closes (30 Nov) and the NE trades set in; the ARC sails in late November, when the risk on its route is very low.
ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

lines: Las Palmas → St Lucia, about 2 700 M
N Atlantic hurricane season: 1 Jun – 30 Nov
NE trades: steady from late Nov–Dec

q: You want to keep cruising the Caribbean through the summer and stay insured. Your policy has this clause. What do you plan?
a: Sail south to Grenada or Trinidad before 1 June
o: Stay in Antigua: storms rarely come before August
Sail north to the Virgin Islands before 1 June
Stay in Antigua with doubled mooring lines
why: The policy decides: be south of the line (Grenada 12°N, Trinidad 10°N) before the exclusion starts, or haul out as agreed.
ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

q: You leave Las Palmas for the Caribbean in December, and the pilot chart for the month gives this. How do you plan the route?
a: Head SSW to about 20°N, then west in the trades
o: The great circle direct: the shortest is fastest
The rhumb line due west along 26–28°N
North-west first, into the westerlies
why: The direct route skirts the Azores high: light winds and calms. Go south till the trades are steady, then turn west.
ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

q: You are in Panama planning the Pacific Puddle Jump and a season in the islands. When do you leave, and when must you be in New Zealand?
a: Leave Feb–Apr; reach New Zealand by early November
o: Leave Sep–Oct; reach New Zealand by March
Leave in June; reach New Zealand by January
Leave in December; reach New Zealand by May
why: Arrive in Polynesia as the cyclone season ends, cruise the austral winter, and be out of the tropics before it starts again.
ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

fig.title: Puddle Jump plan
lines: Then Tahiti, Tonga and on to New Zealand

q: You are crossing the northern Indian Ocean westbound towards the Red Sea. When do you sail?
a: January–February, the NE monsoon behind you
o: July, in the steady SW monsoon
May, in the calm between the monsoons
October, as the SW monsoon eases
why: Westbound you want the NE monsoon astern; the SW monsoon is a gale on the nose, and the changeovers bring cyclones.
ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

q: You leave Bermuda for the Azores in late May, and the high sits across the direct route. Which route do you plan?
a: North of the high to about 38–40°N, then east
o: The rhumb line straight through the high
South of the high, in the NE trades
North to 50°N for the strongest westerlies
why: Round a high on its poleward side for fair westerlies; its centre is calm, its south side is foul easterlies, 50°N is gales.
ref: Ocean passage planning — route and season

q: The rigger’s survey before your Atlantic crossing finds this. What do you do?
a: Re-rig all of it, and carry a spare shroud
o: Replace that one shroud only and go
Tape over the swage and check it daily
Ease that shroud and reef early all the way
why: One crack in 12-year-old wire says the rest is as tired: replace it before 3 weeks of rolling, and carry spare wire and fittings.

fig.title: Rig survey
lines: Cap shroud: hairline crack at lower swage
Rest of the rigging: same age, 12 years

q: You are planning three weeks of trade-wind running with these figures. How do you steer the boat?
a: The windvane day and night; the autopilot as backup
o: The autopilot full-time; run the engine as needed
Hand-steering in 2-hour tricks by all three
The autopilot by day, hand-steering at night
why: Autopilot 6 A × 24 h = 144 Ah + 70 = 214 Ah against 120 Ah: a windvane steers downwind with no power at all.

fig.title: Self-steering
lines: Autopilot, big following sea: 6 A average

q: You are drawing up the energy budget for the crossing from these loads. How much must you put back into the batteries each day?
a: About 206 Ah
o: About 218 Ah
About 278 Ah
About 158 Ah
why: 96 (autopilot) + 5 × 0.4 × 24 = 48 (fridge) + 36 (instruments) + 12 (light) + 14 = 206 Ah a day.

fig.title: Energy budget, per day
lines: Fridge 5.0 A, running 40 % of the time
LED tricolour 1.0 A, 12 h; the rest 14 Ah

q: Ten days out, your energy log settles at these figures. How long do you run the engine each day to keep up?
a: About 1 h 24 min a day
o: About 3 h 36 min a day
About 2 h 12 min a day
None: the 400 Ah bank covers it
why: Deficit 180 − 110 = 70 Ah ÷ 50 A = 1.4 h. The bank’s usable 160 Ah would be gone in about 2 days without it.

q: You are planning drinking water for a 3-week crossing, with washing and dishes done in sea water. What daily allowance do you plan per person?
a: About 3 litres, for drinking and cooking
o: About 1 litre: you drink little at sea
About 10 litres, with fresh-water rinses
About 25 litres, as you use at home
why: Plan about 3 L a person a day for drinking and cooking — more in the tropics — and a reserve on top.
ref: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

q: You are filling up with water for the crossing, as on the card. How much do you carry in cans on top of the tanks?
a: About 55 L in cans
o: None: 350 L covers the 18 days
None: the watermaker makes up any gap
About 135 L in cans
why: 5 × 3 × 18 × 1.5 = 405 L must be aboard without the watermaker: 405 − 350 = 55 L in cans, kept apart from the tanks.
ref: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

fig.title: Water plan
lines: Crew 5; allowance 3 L per person per day
Reserve can’t rely on the watermaker

q: You are writing the provisioning list for the crossing. For how many person-days do you provision?
a: 96 person-days (24 days × 4)
o: 64 person-days (16 days × 4)
80 person-days (16 days × 5)
72 person-days (18 days × 4)
why: 2 000 ÷ 125 = 16 days; +50 % = 24 days for calms and breakdowns; × 4 crew = 96 person-days.
ref: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

q: You are working out your range under power for the crossing. How far can you motor?
a: About 358 M
o: About 477 M
About 248 M
About 330 M
why: 260 L × 0.75 = 195 L ÷ 3.0 L/h = 65 h × 5.5 kn = 358 M, with the reserve still in the tank.

fig.title: Fuel
lines: Diesel: tank 180 L + 4 cans of 20 L
Keep 25 % reserve for landfall and charging

q: You are approaching the doldrums on the way from the Canaries to Brazil. What is your plan for crossing them?
a: Sail every puff, motor only in the calms
o: Motor straight through: the fuel covers 200 M
Motor through, using the 50 L reserve as well
Drift without motoring until the trades fill in
why: 100 L ÷ 3.5 L/h × 6 kn ≈ 171 M — short of 200 M without the reserve; so motor only when the sails can’t do it.

fig.title: Doldrums ahead
lines: ITCZ ahead: about 200 M of calms and squalls

q: A crew applicant for your ocean crossing tells you this. What do you require before you accept them?
a: Double supplies, a backup cool store, a doctor’s plan, a briefed crew
o: Nothing extra: the pump manages it, and they are an adult
Nothing: refuse — no insulin user can sail offshore
Only a letter from their GP saying they are fit
why: A medical condition is planned for, not ignored or barred: spares, insulin kept cool if the fridge fails, a hypo plan, crew who know it.
ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

fig.title: Crew application
lines: Passage 21 days, up to 1 000 M from help

q: You are choosing a watch system for a three-week trade-wind crossing. How many hours on deck does each watchkeeper stand per day in each option?
a: A: 12 h; B: 6 h
o: A: 8 h; B: 6 h
A: 12 h; B: 9 h
A: 6 h; B: 3 h
why: A: half of 24 h each = 12 h. B: 24 h shared by four = 6 h (two 3-h watches) — far more rest over three weeks.
ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

fig.title: Watch systems
lines: Crew of 5: skipper on call, not in the rota
A: two watches of two, 4 on 4 off

q: You set up this rota for a 20-day crossing. Which watches does Anna stand from then on, and what do you change?
a: 0000 and 1200 every day; split one into two dog watches
o: 0000, then 0300 on day 2: it rotates by itself
0000 and 1500 every day; swap pairs each week
0000 and 1200 every day; four can’t be rotated
why: Eight watches a day among four repeat daily (0000, 1200). Split 1800–2100 into two dog watches: nine a day, and the hours rotate.
ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

fig.title: Watch rota
lines: Crew of 4, solo watches of 3 hours

q: At 0310 the AIS shows a tanker passing at CPA 1.6 M. The skipper had a long day. You are on watch with these standing orders. What do you do?
a: Call the skipper now, as the orders say
o: Let him sleep: the tanker will pass clear
Alter course, and tell him in the morning
Call him only if the CPA falls below 1 M
why: Standing orders exist so the watch doesn’t have to judge alone: CPA under 2 M means the skipper is called.
ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

fig.title: Standing orders
lines: Call me: any ship with CPA under 2 M
Call me: wind > 20 kn or baro −3 hPa in 3 h
Clip on at all times at night

q: This is your crew on day 3 of the crossing. What is your first fix as skipper?
a: Guard off-watch sleep, and name a deputy so you sleep too
o: Push on: crews adjust by about day 10
Coffee and double watches until it passes
Heave to every night until everyone is rested
why: Fatigue causes the mistakes: quiet bunks and protected sleep, and a skipper who sleeps — a tired skipper is the biggest risk aboard.
ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

fig.title: Day 3
lines: Two crew can’t sleep off watch
You: 5 hours’ sleep in the last 48

q: This is the mood aboard two weeks into the crossing. What do you do as skipper?
a: A fair duty rota, a crew talk, a halfway treat, a word with the quiet one
o: Keep out of it: adults sort these things out
Give the quiet one the galley to keep them busy
Shorten watches so people see less of each other
why: Morale is the skipper’s job: clear fair duties, air the grievances, mark the halfway, and check privately on anyone withdrawn.
ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

fig.title: Day 14
lines: Rows over galley and clean-up duty

q: Your group of six boats is crossing together and wants a daily check-in with positions and weather, far beyond VHF range and without paying for airtime. What do you set up?
a: A daily HF/SSB net: a set UT time, frequency and controller
o: A VHF channel 72 schedule at 0800 every day
A DSC group call on VHF every evening
AIS text messages to each boat at noon
why: HF (SSB) radio reaches hundreds to thousands of miles free of airtime; VHF and AIS reach only about 20–30 M.

q: You download your GRIB by satellite email each morning mid-ocean. Which request do you send?
a: The route box only: wind and pressure, 1°, 12-hourly to 5 days
o: The whole North Atlantic: 0.25°, hourly to 16 days
The route box: every parameter, 0.25°, hourly to 10 days
The world: wind only, 3-hourly at 0.5° to 7 days
why: At 2.4 kbit/s every kilobyte costs: the area you’ll sail, the fields you use, a coarse grid and days the model can still forecast.

q: You are leaving this float plan ashore before the crossing. What instruction is still missing?
a: When to call the MRCC if reports stop, and which one
o: The crew’s home addresses and employers
A list of the provisions on board
The boat’s insurance renewal date
why: A float plan needs a trigger: e.g. no report for 48 h → call MRCC Falmouth with this plan. Without it the alarm comes late or too soon.

fig.title: Float plan
lines: Shore contact: your sister in Bristol
Plan: boat, crew, raft, EPIRB ID, route, ETA

q: You are checking the navigation pack for this crossing. What do you do about the almanac?
a: Add the 2027 almanac: January isn’t in the 2026 one
o: Nothing: 2026 data is close enough in January
Nothing: the Sun’s data repeats every year
Use the 2026 one and add a day to each date
why: The almanac covers one calendar year: sights after 31 Dec need next year’s (or a long-term) almanac aboard.

q: You are packing the sight reduction tables for this route. Which volumes do you take?
a: Vol 1 and Vol 2
o: Vol 1 only: stars cover every sight
Vol 3 only: Lisbon is near 40°N
Vol 2 and Vol 3, not Vol 1
why: Vol 1 reduces star sights; Vol 2 the Sun, Moon and planets for latitudes 0°–39° — the whole route lies below 39°N.

q: This is the state of the boat after a night of thunderstorms. What is your navigation plan for the rest of the crossing?
a: Handheld GPS fixes a few times a day, sights as a check, a paper DR
o: DR only, until the plotter is repaired ashore
The handheld GPS left on full-time; the sextant stays boxed
A position from the MRCC by sat phone each day
why: The backup chain: the handheld (kept in the oven from the lightning), used sparingly for its batteries, with celestial and DR behind it.

fig.title: After the lightning
lines: In the oven: handheld GPS and batteries

q: This is your daily routine on the crossing. Which check is still missing from it?
a: A compass check by the Sun’s amplitude or azimuth
o: A second GRIB download each midnight
An hourly sounding of the water tanks
A weekly check of the chart datum
why: On an ocean passage the compass is checked daily (sunrise or sunset amplitude, or an azimuth) and the error logged.

fig.title: Daily routine
lines: 0700 UT: GRIB download, check the routing
Noon: noon position and the day’s run
Daily: water, fuel and battery state

o: 11 Dec, about 0410
11 Dec, about 2210
10 Dec, about 1120

q: You are reviewing the medical kit for the crossing. What do you add?
a: Prescription drugs and a medical guide, agreed with a doctor
o: More plasters and bandages: the same kit doubled
Nothing: radio advice replaces a bigger kit
A defibrillator in place of extra medicines
why: Days from help, you must treat, not just patch: antibiotics, strong painkillers, wound closure — chosen with a doctor, with a guide.

a: Call the MRCC for radio medical advice from a doctor
o: Call PAN-PAN on VHF channel 16 for any ship
Give antibiotics and painkillers, then wait 24 h
Head for the nearest port and tell nobody yet
why: Mid-ocean the MRCC connects you to a telemedical doctor (TMAS) by sat phone or HF, and arranges help if evacuation is needed.

q: This is Tom on the first day of the crossing. What do you do?
a: Off the rota; in the cockpit, clipped on, sipping fluids
o: Send him below to his bunk in the bow
Keep him on watch: it passes faster that way
Give him a big meal to settle his stomach
why: Seasick crew are a MOB and dehydration risk: off watch, warm, clipped on in the cockpit (or aft bunk), small sips, watch their fluids.

lines: Tom: vomiting for 6 hours, cold, quiet

a: B, with the >24 h pack
o: A, with the <24 h pack
C: the dinghy is enough
A, with a bigger grab bag
why: Rescue may take days far offshore: an offshore raft with the >24 h (SOLAS-style) pack — water, food, flares, a sea anchor.

lines: B: ISO 9650-1 Group A, >24 h pack

q: You bought this boat in the summer and are preparing her for the crossing. What do you do about the EPIRB?
a: Recode and register it for Malta, and renew the battery
o: Nothing: any 406 MHz beacon alerts the MRCC
Renew the battery; registration doesn’t matter
Register it for Malta; the old battery still works
why: The MRCC uses the registration to call your contacts and know the boat; an expired battery may not last the 48 h a rescue needs.

fig.title: EPIRB check
lines: EPIRB: registered to the previous owner, UK
Today: Nov 2026; boat now on the Malta flag

q: You are equipping the lifejackets of your crew of four for an ocean crossing. Which device on each lifejacket gets your own boat back to a person overboard at night fastest?
a: An AIS MOB beacon, seen on your own plotter
o: A 406 MHz PLB, alerting the MRCC
A personal strobe light on its own
A whistle and retro-reflective tape
why: Mid-ocean the rescue is your own boat: an AIS MOB beacon alarms and shows the casualty on your plotter; a PLB alerts an MRCC days away.

q: At 0200 in 20 kn of trade wind a halyard fouls at the masthead and you must go forward. What do you do?
a: Wake a second crew and clip on before leaving the hatch
o: Go quickly unclipped: it takes a minute
Clip on once you reach the mast
Clip to the guardrail as you go forward
why: Far from help you cannot count on recovery: the jackstay from the companionway, a second person awake, a lifejacket and a light.

q: This happens on your night watch in the trades. What are your first actions?
a: MOB button, danbuoy and light, a pointer, then the kite down
o: Gybe at once under the kite, back to him
MAYDAY first, then turn when the MRCC replies
Keep sailing while you plan a search pattern
why: At 8 kn you lose 250 m a minute: mark the spot, give him a buoy, keep eyes on him, then drop the spinnaker and return under power.

fig.title: Man overboard!
lines: Crew of 4; one overboard, with a light

q: This is the situation aboard. What do you do?
a: Stay aboard, fight the leak, alert the MRCC; the raft only if she sinks
o: Abandon now, while it is calm and daylight
Set off the EPIRB and step into the raft
Wait for the leak to ease, and alert no one
why: The boat is the best liferaft: step up into the raft only when she is going down. Tell the MRCC early (PAN-PAN) and keep pumping.

fig.title: Day 12: leak
lines: Leak at a seacock; water rising slowly
Electric and manual pumps keep up

q: This is your coastal grab bag. What do you add for an ocean crossing, with rescue possibly days away?
a: A PLB, a sat phone, water and a hand watermaker
o: More flares and a second handheld VHF
A bigger first-aid kit and more torches
Fishing gear and a book for the wait
why: Days in a raft mid-ocean: water first (a hand watermaker), a way to alert (PLB/EPIRB) and to talk to the MRCC (sat phone).

fig.title: Grab bag (coastal)
lines: Passports, phone in a dry bag

q: You are approaching an atoll in the Tuamotus. What speed do you make good from now?
a: About 3.0 kn: reef down, or heave to for part of the night
o: About 6.0 kn: in the pass by midnight
About 4.0 kn: at the pass at 0400
About 2.0 kn: the pass at 1600 tomorrow
why: 1600 to 0800 is 16 h: 48 M ÷ 16 h = 3.0 kn. At 7 kn you’d be at an unlit reef pass at about 2250.

fig.title: Landfall timing
lines: Plan: in the pass at 0800, sun high
No lights; charts from old surveys

q: You are making a night landfall after 19 days at sea. At about what range do you expect to raise this light?
a: About 18 M
o: About 26 M
About 15 M
About 30 M
why: Geographical range 2.08 × (√52 + √2.5) = 2.08 × 8.79 ≈ 18 M: the curve of the Earth hides it before its 26 M nominal range.

q: You are sailing between low atolls at night. How do you navigate this stretch?

o: Trust the plotter: GPS is good to 5 m
Close to 1 M to see the reef in the moonlight
Steer the plotter’s waypoint through the gap
why: GPS is precise but the old chart may be offset by a mile, and the current is unknown: keep a wide margin and pass in daylight.

Anchor in a quiet bay first, clear in later
why: Arriving from abroad: straight to a port of entry, the yellow Q flag flying, and nobody ashore until cleared, except to clear in.

o: Your Yachtmaster logbook of miles sailed
The liferaft’s last service certificate
A fishing licence for the crossing

Lie ahull: all sail down, helm lashed
Carry on as fast as she will go downwind

Motor head to wind all night
Run back 100 M the way you came

Mid-November, with the other ARC boats

lines: Trade-wind sun: about 5 peak hours a day

q: You are working out how far you can motor in calms on the crossing, as on the card. What range do you plan?
a: About 309 M
o: About 450 M
About 386 M
About 373 M

fig.title: Fuel plan
lines: Charging: 1.5 h a day at 1.2 L/h, 20 days

q: Your boat has wheel steering, and you are preparing her for an ocean crossing. Which steering check do you do with the crew in harbour?
a: Fit the emergency tiller and steer with it
o: Turn the wheel from lock to lock once
Check the autopilot shows the heading
Grease the wheel brake and the pedestal
why: A broken cable or quadrant mid-ocean means steering by the emergency tiller: fit it and use it before you need it, and know where it is.

q: This is what you find on your morning deck check. What do you do?
a: End-for-end it, pad the pole end, ease it a little daily
o: Tape it over and leave it until the Caribbean
Roll the genoa away and sail on under main
Sheet it in hard so it stops moving
why: Weeks on one tack wear through anything: move the chafe point every day (“freshen the nip”), pad it, and check every morning.

fig.title: Morning deck check
lines: Genoa sheet half worn through at the pole
Same chafe point since the start

q: You are checking the engine spares before the crossing, as on the card. What do you add?
a: Fuel filters, an impeller and an alternator belt
o: A spare propeller and a shaft seal
A second gasket set and more oil
Nothing: 30 hours of running needs no spares
why: Your charging depends on the engine: carry what fails at sea — fuel filters (dirty diesel), raw-water impellers and belts.

fig.title: Engine spares
lines: Engine: 1.5 h a day for charging, 20 days
Spares box: oil, one fuel filter, gaskets

q: You run this watch system on a crossing with a crew of six. Which watches does A stand from 1900 on day 2?
why: Five watches a day, taken in turn by two teams: A stands 1st, 3rd, 5th on day 1, then 2nd and 4th — so the times swap daily.
ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

fig.title: Watch bill
lines: Swedish system, two watches A and B

q: Your crew of six will stand in two watches of three for four weeks. You want short watches at night and watch times that change from day to day. Which system do you choose?
a: Swedish: five a day, 4 h at night and 6 h by day
o: 4 on, 4 off: six watches of 4 h a day
6 on, 6 off: four watches of 6 h a day
3 on, 3 off: eight watches of 3 h a day
why: With two teams the times rotate only if the day has an odd number of watches; the Swedish five do, with short night ones.
ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

q: You are taking three crew you met on a crewing website across the Atlantic. What do you do before you commit to the passage with them?
a: A shakedown of two or three days offshore, with night watches
o: An afternoon sail in the bay to see them handle the boat
An interview and their references; the sea will do the rest
Nothing: their sailing certificates say what they can do
why: Only a few days and nights at sea show seasickness, skill and character — while you can still change crew or fix the boat.
ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

q: This is what your 48-hour shakedown sail shows. Whom do you leave ashore for the crossing?
a: Carl: he ignores the standing orders
o: Ana: her seasickness rules her out
Ben: he has no ocean miles
No one: all three will settle in
why: Seasickness passes and keenness learns; a crew who won’t follow the clip-on rule is a risk to himself and to everyone who goes back for him.
ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

fig.title: Shakedown, 48 h offshore
lines: Ana: seasick day 1, on watch again day 2
Carl: 2 crossings; unclipped twice at night

q: You write the night orders for the rest of the crossing after this. Which order prevents it happening again?
a: No spinnaker after dark; call me for any squall
o: Hand-steer whenever the spinnaker is up
Radar off at night to save the batteries
Two on watch after midnight, kite or not
why: Trade-wind squalls come at night and can double the wind: a night sail plan you can hold in one, and the skipper called early.
ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

fig.title: Night watch, 0200
lines: 0200: squall line astern on the radar
Watch: “the last ones were only 25 kn”

q: You are handing over the watch at 0300 and have said this. What else does the new watch need from you?
a: The barometer trend and any squalls you have seen
o: The day’s run so far and the ETA
The water left in the tanks
The engine hours since the service
why: A handover gives what the next watch must act on: course and sails, traffic, and what the weather is doing — pressure and squalls.
ref: Ocean passage planning — crew and watches

fig.title: Watch handover, 0300
lines: One reef in, genoa poled out
Ship astern on AIS, overtaking, CPA 2.5 M

q: A crew who gets seasick tells you they will take a tablet “if I start to feel ill” once you are out of Las Palmas. What do you tell them?
a: Take it before we leave, as the leaflet directs
o: Wait until you are sick, then take two
Skip it: the body adapts in the first hour
Take it with a big meal after your first watch
why: Seasickness tablets prevent rather than cure: start them before departure, at the time the leaflet gives; once vomiting starts they stay down poorly.

q: You are about to call for radio medical advice, as on the card. What do you have ready before you call?
a: Position, pulse, breathing, temperature, history, the kit list
o: Only the position: the doctor asks the rest later
The insurance policy number and his passport
Nothing: call first, then examine him
why: The doctor can only work from what you report: vital signs, what happened, medicines given or allergies, and what your kit holds.

fig.title: Day 11: injury
lines: Day 11: crew fell against a winch
Sat phone; MRCC will connect a doctor

q: Your crew have been saving water, as on the card. What do you do?
a: Raise the ration to 3–4 L, with rehydration salts
o: Keep the ration: the water has to last
Give seasickness tablets and rest
Let them rinse their faces in sea water
why: These are signs of dehydration. 260 L ÷ (4 × 9) ≈ 7 L a person a day: there is water to drink 3–4 L in the tropics.

fig.title: Day 10: dehydration?
lines: Day 10, 28 °C; crew rationing 2 L a day
Water aboard: 260 L; 9 days to go; crew 4

q: You are at the market in Las Palmas, buying fresh food for a 3-week crossing with no room in the fridge. Which basket lasts into the third week?
a: Basket B
o: Basket A
Basket C
Basket D
why: Hard vegetables, onions, potatoes and unwashed, unrefrigerated eggs keep for weeks; soft and ripe food lasts days.
ref: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

fig.title: Market, Las Palmas
lines: B: cabbage, onions, potatoes, unwashed eggs

q: You are stowing the fresh food for the crossing, as on the card. How do you stow it?
a: Dry and airy, wrapped singly, checked daily
o: Sealed in plastic bags in the cool bilge
All together in one deep locker
Washed and stowed damp in a hanging net
why: Air and dryness keep it; one rotten fruit spoils its neighbours. A whole stem of bananas ripens at once — buy hands at different stages.
ref: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

fig.title: Fresh food aboard
lines: No fridge space; 3 weeks to go

q: One of your water tanks is contaminated, as on the card. What daily ration do you set per person?
a: About 2.5 L each a day
o: About 3.1 L each a day
About 5.5 L each a day
About 1.5 L each a day
why: Clean water 125 + 25 = 150 L, less 20 % = 120 L ÷ (4 × 12) = 2.5 L. This is why the water is split between tanks and cans.
ref: Ocean passage planning — provisions and water

fig.title: Day 8: water
lines: Day 8 of 20 expected: 12 days to go
Port tank (180 L) tastes of diesel: shut off
Clean: starboard tank 125 L + cans 25 L

q: This is your situation, with 10 days still to go. How do you get the weather from now on?
a: HF weatherfax charts and high-seas forecasts on the SSB
o: The old GRIB: it runs out to 16 days
NAVTEX: it carries the high-seas forecast here
Ask passing ships on VHF once a day
why: The SSB receiver needs no airtime: surface analyses and forecasts by HF fax, the high-seas bulletin by voice — with your barometer log.

fig.title: Day 9: no sat phone
lines: Day 9, mid-Atlantic: the sat phone is dead
SSB receiver and a laptop with a fax app
NAVTEX receiver; VHF; 1 100 M to land

q: You want the official high-seas forecasts and navigational warnings on the whole route, as on the card. What do you fit?
a: An Inmarsat-C (EGC) receiver for SafetyNET
o: A second NAVTEX receiver, as a spare
A VHF radio with DSC
An AIS receiver with a chart display
why: SafetyNET broadcasts the high-seas forecasts and warnings by satellite to EGC receivers ocean-wide; NAVTEX reaches only a few hundred miles.

fig.title: Weather backup
lines: Sat phone: GRIB by email (can fail)
NAVTEX on board: coastal range only
Route: 2 800 M, far from any coast

q: You are mid-Atlantic, westbound, and keep the ship’s clocks to the zone, as on the card. At what ship’s time do you send the report?
a: 1400 ship’s time
o: 2200 ship’s time
1800 ship’s time
1000 ship’s time
why: Zone +4: UT = zone time + 4 h, so zone time = 1800 − 4 = 1400. Keep reports in UT so the shore never has to guess.

q: It is 0700 UT on day 12, and you are all well, as on the card. What do you do?
a: Ask a boat on the HF net to email home that all is well
o: Nothing: the MRCC can see you are fine on AIS
Set off the EPIRB briefly so they get your position
Turn for the nearest port to phone home
why: The 48-h trigger falls at 1800 UT today: relay a short report before then, or a needless search starts. Never use the EPIRB as a message.

fig.title: Day 12: silence
lines: Day 12: the sat phone dead since day 10
Shore plan: no report for 48 h → call MRCC
HF net at 0800 UT; a boat on it has email

q: A crew member suggests this mid-ocean. What do you do?
a: Keep it transmitting: ships and satellites see you
o: Silent mode: receiving them is all you need
Transmit at night only, silent by day
Switch it off and keep a radar watch
why: 0.4 A × 24 h ≈ 10 Ah, a small part of the budget: ships see you at night, and the satellite AIS track helps a search if needed.

fig.title: AIS mid-ocean
lines: Crew: “Switch the AIS to silent, save power”
Shipping: 2–3 ships a day on the route

q: You are about to send this daily report to your shore contact. What must you add?
a: Position, course, speed and the next report time
o: The menu and the fish you have caught
The crew’s moods and the watch rota
The engine hours and the fuel used
why: A report must let the shore and the MRCC find you and know when to worry: UT, position, course and speed, conditions, next report.

fig.title: Daily report
lines: “flying fish for breakfast. Love to all.”

q: You are writing the navigation routine for an ocean crossing with a working GPS and plotter. How often do you check the steering compass?
a: Daily at sunrise or sunset, and after a big change of heading
o: Once before leaving: deviation doesn’t change at sea
Only if the GPS fails, to find the error then
Weekly at noon, from the Sun’s meridian altitude
why: Log the compass error daily (amplitude or azimuth) on the heading you steer: if the GPS fails you need it for steering and DR.

q: You are checking the navigation pack for the crossing, as on the card. What do you add for the landfall?
a: A large-scale paper chart and a pilot book for the approach
o: A second ocean chart, in case one gets wet
More plotting sheets for the last 100 M
A star chart for night arrivals
why: The ocean chart can’t show a harbour: if the plotter fails at landfall you need the approach and harbour on paper, with the lights.

q: At the noon position you check whether the crew will make their flights. What daily run must you average from now?
a: About 137 M a day (5.7 kn)
o: About 126 M a day (5.3 kn)
About 149 M a day (6.2 kn)
About 164 M a day (6.8 kn)
why: Noon 18 Dec to noon 30 Dec is 12 days: 1 640 ÷ 12 ≈ 137 M a day, or 5.7 kn.

fig.title: Noon, 18 December
lines: Crew flights: must arrive by noon 30 Dec

q: You are writing the day’s run in the log, as on the card. What average speed do you enter?
a: 6.0 kn
why: Putting the clocks back makes this noon-to-noon day 25 hours long: 150 M ÷ 25 h = 6.0 kn.

fig.title: Day’s run
lines: Westbound; clocks put back 1 h at midnight
Noon yesterday to noon today (ship’s time)

q: You want to stop the boat and let everyone sleep, lying bow to the seas, as on the card. What do you stream, and from where?
a: The parachute sea anchor, from the bow
o: The series drogue, from the bow
The parachute sea anchor, from the stern
The series drogue astern, and keep running
why: A sea anchor from the bow holds her head to the seas almost stopped; a drogue astern only slows her while she runs on.

fig.title: Gale: stopping
lines: 45 kn, breaking seas; crew of 3 exhausted
Sea room: 600 M in every direction
Aboard: series drogue, parachute sea anchor

q: You are among the atolls when this gale arrives. How do you ride it out?
a: Lie to the sea anchor from the bow
o: Heave to and keep a good watch
Run off before it with the drogue
Lie ahull, with everything lashed
why: Hove to: 1.8 kn × 30 h = 54 M — on the reef after 20 h. On the sea anchor: 0.4 × 30 = 12 M, well short of it.

fig.title: Gale near the reefs
lines: Gale from the north, about 30 h to come
Drift on the sea anchor: 0.4 kn

q: You are back alongside your man overboard, as on the card. How do you get him aboard?
a: A halyard to his lifting loop, and winch him up
o: Both haul him over the guardrail by his arms
Drop the ladder and tell him to climb
Tow him astern to calmer water first
why: A cold, exhausted casualty can’t climb, and two people can’t lift 90 kg up 1.2 m: a halyard and a winch can — horizontally if you can.

fig.title: Recovery
lines: Freeboard 1.2 m; two of you left aboard
His lifejacket has a lifting loop

q: You must abandon the boat, as on the card. In what order do you do it?
a: MAYDAY, painter made fast, raft over, step in dry, cut free
o: Raft over, jump in, then the MAYDAY from the raft
Raft over, then make the painter fast as it inflates
Cut the painter at once to drift clear of the fire
why: Alert first (MAYDAY, EPIRB), secure the painter before launching or the raft blows away, board from the deck, then cut.

fig.title: Abandon ship
lines: Grab bag and EPIRB by the hatch

q: Your liferaft’s service record reads like this, a few weeks before the crossing. What do you do?
a: Have it serviced before you leave
o: Go: a sealed raft lasts ten years
Have it serviced in the Caribbean
Open it on deck to check it yourself
why: Overdue by a year: the gas, pack and seals are no longer certified. The raft you may live in for days is serviced before departure.

q: You are planning the landfall at an atoll, as on the card. What do you do?
a: Ease to about 5 kn, at the pass soon after dawn
o: Keep 6 kn and enter at about 2340 by GPS
Motor-sail at 7 kn to be in before sunset
Heave to for 24 h now, then sail in at 6 kn
why: At 6 kn: 214 ÷ 6 = 36 h, the pass at 2340 tomorrow. Sunset needs 7.1 kn for 30 h; 0630 the day after needs 214 ÷ 42.5 h ≈ 5 kn.

fig.title: Landfall timing
lines: Noon: 214 M to the reef pass
Best speed in this wind: 6.0 kn
Pass: daylight only; diesel for 8 h

q: Your GPS has failed and your position comes from sun sights, good to about 8 M. You are closing this low, featureless coast. Where do you aim?
a: Point B, 15 M up-current of the harbour
o: Point A, the harbour itself
Point C, 15 M down-current of the harbour
Midway between A and C
why: Aim off deliberately: at landfall you know the harbour is south, and you run down to it with the current, not search both ways.

q: You are planning a landfall in a remote island group, as on the card. How do you plan it?
a: As if unlit: stand off and close the coast by day
o: Steer for the light’s charted position on the plotter
Close to 3 M of the coast and look for it
Enter on the light: it is on the chart
why: In remote groups lights fail and go unrepaired: plan the landfall without them, keep offshore in the dark and close the land in daylight.

fig.title: Remote landfall
lines: are often unlit or off station”

q: You email your arrival notice to Tongan customs before leaving Niue, as on the card. What ETA do you give?
a: 12 June, about 1000
o: 11 June, about 1000
10 June, about 1000
11 June, about 2100
why: Leave 9 June 1900 UT; + 50 h = 11 June 2100 UT; Tonga (+13) = 12 June 1000. Same clock time, but a day later across the date line.

fig.title: Niue → Tonga
lines: Customs want the ETA in Tonga time

q: You are sailing to Australia, as on the card. When do you send the advance notice of arrival?
a: Before you leave Nouméa
o: Halfway across, by sat phone email
On arrival, from the quarantine dock
Within 24 h of arriving
why: 96 hours is four days — about the whole passage: the notice goes in before departure, or you arrive unannounced and face penalties.

fig.title: Arrival notice
lines: Border Force: notice ≥ 96 h before arrival

q: You have cleared in, as on the card. What do you do before Jo leaves?
a: Sign Jo off the crew list with immigration
o: Nothing: once cleared, crew come and go
Let Jo go and fix the list when you clear out
Give Jo the boat’s papers for the airport
why: The skipper answers for everyone on the crew list: sign a leaving crew off with immigration, or you may have to explain a missing person.

fig.title: Crew change
lines: Cleared in at Bridgetown: 5 crew on the list
Immigration: crew stay on the boat’s list
The rest sail on to Grenada next week

q: Customs and immigration have cleared you in at Horta, in the Azores. What do you do with the flags?
a: Q flag down; Portuguese courtesy flag at the starboard spreader
o: Leave the Q flag up until you leave the country
Courtesy flag at the port spreader, Q flag above it
Your own ensign at the starboard spreader
why: The Q flag says you are not yet cleared; once cleared it comes down and the host country’s courtesy flag goes up to starboard.

q: Your new storm trysail and storm jib have never been set. When do you try them?
a: In harbour or a fresh breeze before you leave
o: The first time a gale comes
Never: a deep-reefed main does the job
Halfway across, on a calm day
why: In a gale is no time to find the track won’t take the slides or the sheets don’t lead: rig and set them before departure.

q: You are preparing for the gale, as on the card. What else do you do now?
a: Lash all below, food in flasks, crew rested
o: Motor at full speed to outrun the gale
Take out the washboards for ventilation
Drop all sail now and lie ahull
why: Before a gale: everything heavy secured below, hot food and drink ready, the crew fed and asleep in turn — tired crew make the mistakes.

fig.title: Gale in 12 h
lines: Done: two reefs, storm jib hanked on

q: The MRCC asks if you can help, as on the card. What do you do?
a: Go: you must assist if you can do so safely
o: Decline: the ship will be there in 20 hours
Decline: a racing yacht may carry on
Relay the call and hold your course
why: A skipper must go to people in distress when able to without serious danger to their own boat; the race and the place come second.

fig.title: Call from the MRCC
lines: Rally day 8; you lie 3rd in your class
MRCC: dismasted yacht 55 M upwind, injured
Your crew of 5: rested, boat sound

q: This is your situation after the evacuation. How do you sail on?
a: Short watches, less sail at night, AIS and radar alarms set
o: Both sleep at night with the AIS alarm on
Full sail day and night to finish fast
Turn back 900 M upwind to the start
why: Two can sail on with care: shorter watches so neither is worn out, a sail plan one person can handle, alarms backing up the lookout.

fig.title: After the evacuation
lines: Two crew taken off by a ship after injury
Left aboard: you and one crew
